title: Culmen fractum. Mors Priami
titleEn: The Fall of Priam's Palace — Aeneid II.486–587
about: Inside the palace the women's cries beat against the golden stars; frightened mothers wander the great halls, clasping the doorposts and pressing kisses on them. Pyrrhus presses on with his father's force; neither bars nor guards can hold, the door totters under the ram, the posts are wrenched from their hinge, and the Danaans pour in, kill the first they meet and fill the place with soldiers. Not even a foaming river that breaks its dykes and carries off herds and stalls rushes so furiously. Aeneas saw Neoptolemus mad with slaughter, the two Atridae at the threshold, Hecuba and her hundred daughters-in-law, and Priam fouling with his blood the very fires he had hallowed; the fifty bridal chambers and the doorposts proud with barbarian gold lie fallen, and the Greeks hold whatever the fire spares. Then Aeneas tells Priam's fate. Seeing the city taken, the threshold torn and the enemy in the heart of his house, the old man buckles long-disused arms on his trembling shoulders in vain and sets out to die among the foe. In the middle of the house, under the open sky, stand a great altar and an ancient laurel overshadowing the household gods; there Hecuba and her daughters crouch like doves driven by a black storm, clasping the images of the gods. When she sees Priam in a young man's arms she cries out: what resolve has driven him to gird on such weapons, and where is he rushing? Such help and such defenders the hour does not need, not even if her own Hector were here; let him come to the altar, which will shelter them all, or he will die with them. She takes the old man to her and seats him in the holy place. Then Polites, one of Priam's sons, escapes from Pyrrhus' slaughter and flees wounded through spears and enemies along the long colonnades and empty halls, with Pyrrhus blazing after him, now and now almost with his spear in him. When he reaches the sight and faces of his parents he falls and pours out his life with much blood. Priam, though held in the midst of death, does not hold back voice or anger: may the gods, if there is any justice in heaven, give the man who made him look on his son's death and defiled a father's face the reward that is due; Achilles, whose son Pyrrhus falsely claims to be, was not such to Priam his enemy, but respected a suppliant's rights and trust, gave back Hector's bloodless body for burial and sent him home. So saying he hurls a weak spear without force; the hoarse bronze turns it and it hangs from the shield's boss. Pyrrhus tells him to carry the news to his father Achilles, to tell him of his deeds and of the degenerate Neoptolemus, and says: 'Now die.' He drags the trembling old man, slipping in his son's blood, to the very altar, winds his left hand in his hair and drives the sword to the hilt into his side. So ended the destiny of Priam, who had seen Troy burn and Pergamum fall, once the proud ruler of so many peoples and lands of Asia: a huge trunk lies there, a head torn from the shoulders, a body without a name. Then a savage horror closes round Aeneas. He is stunned; the image of his dear father rises before him as he sees a king of his father's age breathing out his life from a cruel wound; he thinks of Creusa left alone, the plundered house and the danger of little Iulus. He looks round for his men and finds that all, worn out, have left him, some flinging their bodies to the ground, others giving them up to the flames. Greenough prints the last stretch of the part, 567–587, within square brackets as spurious: Aeneas, left alone, sees Helen hiding in silence at the threshold of Vesta's shrine, lit by the bright fires, in dread of the Trojans angry at the fall of Troy, of the Greeks' vengeance and of the wrath of the husband she deserted, a common Fury to Troy and to her own country. Anger blazes up in him to avenge his falling country and exact a criminal's penalty. 'Is she to see Sparta and Mycenae safe, go home as queen in a triumph she has won, and see husband, house, parents and children with a crowd of Trojan women and Phrygian servants? Is Priam to have died by the sword, Troy to have burned, the Dardan shore to have sweated so often with blood? No: though there is no famous name in punishing a woman, and no praise in such a victory, I shall be praised for wiping out an abomination and exacting the due penalty, and it will be a joy to have filled my soul with avenging flame and satisfied the ashes of my own.'

sentences.i: But within, the house is all confusion, groans and wretched uproar, and deep in the hollow halls the lament of women rings out;
sentences.n: A new paragraph; Aeneas is telling Dido how the palace fell. 'gemitu miseroque tumultu' are ablatives of means with 'miscetur' (passive, 'is thrown into confusion'). 'cavae aedes' is the subject of 'ululant', a plural verb, and 'plangoribus femineis' is an ablative of means or manner, 'with womanly lamentations' (the 'planctus' was the beating of the breast). 'penitus' is an adverb, 'deep within'.

sentences.t: ferit aurea sidera clamor.
sentences.l: strikes the golden stars the clamour.
sentences.i: the din strikes the golden stars.
sentences.n: 'aurea sidera' is a conventional epithet; the stars are 'golden'. 'ferit' is singular, agreeing with 'clamor', its subject, although the sentence began with the plural 'aedes'. The hyperbole of a cry reaching the stars is a favourite device of epic.

sentences.t: Tum pavidae tectis matres ingentibus errant;
sentences.l: Then the frightened mothers through the huge buildings wander;
sentences.i: Then frightened mothers wander through the vast rooms;
sentences.n: 'tectis ingentibus' is an ablative of the place where without 'in', common in poetry. 'matres' is 'mothers', that is, the women of the house; 'pavidae' agrees with it.

sentences.t: amplexaeque tenent postis atque oscula figunt.
sentences.l: and embracing they hold the doorposts and press kisses on them.
sentences.i: and clasp the doorposts, hold fast to them, and press kisses on them.
sentences.n: 'amplexae' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'amplector', used with present sense, 'embracing' (you'll see this constantly). 'postis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is (you'll see this constantly); at 493 he prints 'postes'. 'figunt' means 'fix', 'plant' kisses; 'tenent' and 'figunt' go with the same subject, 'matres'.

sentences.t: Instat vi patria Pyrrhus;
sentences.l: Presses on with his father's force Pyrrhus;
sentences.i: Pyrrhus presses on with all his father's might;
sentences.n: Pyrrhus is Achilles' son, also called Neoptolemus (500). 'vi patria' is an ablative of manner, 'with his father's force'. 'instat' is 'presses on'.

sentences.t:
nec claustra, neque ipsi
custodes sufferre valent;
sentences.l:
not the bars, nor the guards themselves
are able to withstand;
sentences.i: neither the bars nor the guards themselves can hold out against him;
sentences.n: 'nec… neque' pair two negatives, 'neither… nor' (Greenough prints 'neque'; the Latin Library 'nec', which makes no difference to the sense). 'sufferre' is an infinitive with 'valent' and has no object stated; the force of Pyrrhus is understood. 'ipsi custodes' are 'the guards themselves'.

sentences.t:
labat ariete crebro
ianua, et emoti procumbunt cardine postes.
sentences.l:
totters under the ram, repeated,
the door, and torn out of the hinge fall forward the doorposts.
sentences.i: Under the ram's repeated blows the door gives way, and the posts, wrenched from their hinge, crash forward.
sentences.n: 'ariete crebro' is an ablative of means, 'with the frequent ram' (a battering-ram). 'emoti' is a perfect passive participle, 'dislodged', and 'cardine' an ablative of separation, 'from the hinge'. 'postes' here means the leaves or jambs of the door.

sentences.t: Fit via vi;
sentences.l: Is made a way by force;
sentences.i: A way is forced;
sentences.n: 'Fit via vi' is a play on sound. 'fit' is the passive of 'facio', 'is made'; 'vi' is an ablative of means, 'by force'.

sentences.t:
rumpunt aditus, primosque trucidant
immissi Danai, et late loca milite complent.
sentences.l:
they break the entrances, and the first they slaughter,
sent in, the Danaans, and widely the places with soldiery fill.
sentences.i: The Greeks, let loose, break through the entrances, cut down the first they meet, and fill the whole place with armed men.
sentences.n: 'immissi' is a perfect passive participle, 'let in, let loose', agreeing with 'Danai'. 'primos' is the object of 'trucidant', 'the first (men)'. 'milite' is a collective singular ablative of means, 'with soldiery'. 'late' is an adverb, 'far and wide'.

sentences.t:
Non sic, aggeribus ruptis cum spumeus amnis
exiit, oppositasque evicit gurgite moles,
fertur in arva furens cumulo, camposque per omnis
cum stabulis armenta trahit.
sentences.l:
Not so, embankments burst when the foaming river
has gone out, and the obstructing barriers has overcome with its eddy,
it is borne on the fields raging in a heap, and the plains through all
with the stalls the herds drags.
sentences.i: Less fiercely than this, when a foaming river bursts its banks, beats down the barriers set against it with its surge, and sweeps raging over the fields in a mounded flood, dragging herds and stalls across every plain.
sentences.n: A simile: the flood of the Greeks. 'Non sic' looks forward: the river is carried over the fields (the verb is 'fertur', 497–498) not as fiercely as the Greeks pour into the house. 'cum' with the perfect indicative 'exiit' (and 'evicit') means 'when' the river 'has burst out'. 'aggeribus ruptis' is an ablative absolute, 'the dykes broken'. 'oppositas moles' are 'the barriers set in its way'. 'cumulo' is an ablative of manner, 'in a heap', that is, in a mass of water. 'omnis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is, and 'per' stands after its noun ('camposque per omnis'). 'trahit' is singular, with 'armenta' as object and 'cum stabulis' 'along with the stalls'. The picture is Homeric; compare Iliad 5 and 11 for rivers in spate.

sentences.t:
Vidi ipse furentem
caede Neoptolemum geminosque in limine Atridas;
sentences.l:
I saw myself raging
with slaughter Neoptolemus and the twin Atridae on the threshold;
sentences.i: I saw it with my own eyes: Neoptolemus mad with slaughter, and the two Atridae at the threshold;
sentences.n: Aeneas speaks as an eyewitness ('Vidi ipse'). 'furentem' is a present participle agreeing with 'Neoptolemum', and 'caede' is an ablative of cause, 'with slaughter'. Neoptolemus is Pyrrhus. 'Atridas' is the Greek accusative plural, 'the sons of Atreus', Agamemnon and Menelaus; 'geminos' is 'twin' in the sense of 'the pair'.

sentences.t:
vidi Hecubam centumque nurus, Priamumque per aras
sanguine foedantem, quos ipse sacraverat, ignis.
sentences.l:
I saw Hecuba and a hundred daughters-in-law, and Priam through the altars
with blood defiling, which himself he had consecrated, the fires.
sentences.i: I saw Hecuba and her hundred daughters-in-law, and Priam among the altars fouling with his blood the very fires he had himself hallowed.
sentences.n: 'vidi' is repeated at the start of the line for emphasis (anaphora, with 499). 'centum nurus' is a round number for Priam's many sons' wives (and daughters). 'foedantem' is a present participle agreeing with 'Priamum', 'defiling'. The relative clause 'quos ipse sacraverat' comes before its antecedent, 'ignis', here the sacred fires of the altars (Greenough's accusative plural in -is). 'sacraverat' is a pluperfect, 'had consecrated'.

sentences.i: Those fifty bridal chambers, a hope of grandchildren so great, and the doorposts proud with foreign gold and trophies, lay in ruins;
sentences.n: 'procubuere' is the perfect 'procubuerunt' (-ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly), the verb for the subjects 'thalami… postes'. Priam had fifty sons, each with a chamber in the palace, the 'hope of grandsons'. 'barbarico auro spoliisque' are ablatives of cause with 'superbi', 'proud of'; 'barbaricus' here means 'foreign, Eastern', not rude.

sentences.t: tenent Danai, qua deficit ignis.
sentences.l: hold the Danaans, where fails the fire.
sentences.i: the Greeks hold whatever the fire has spared.
sentences.n: 'tenent' has the Danaans as subject, with the places of the palace as object understood. 'qua' is a relative adverb, 'where', and 'deficit' means 'gives out, fails'; so the Greeks hold everything the fire has not yet taken.

sentences.t: Forsitan et Priami fuerint quae fata requiras.
sentences.l: Perhaps also of Priam what fates there were you may ask.
sentences.i: You may well ask, too, what befell Priam.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Forsitan' (= 'fors sit an', 'perhaps') takes the subjunctive 'requiras', 'you may ask' (Aeneas addresses Dido). 'quae fata fuerint' is an indirect question, 'what the fates of Priam were'; 'et' means 'also'.

sentences.t:
Urbis uti captae casum convolsaque vidit
limina tectorum et medium in penetralibus hostem,
arma diu senior desueta trementibus aevo
circumdat nequiquam umeris, et inutile ferrum
cingitur, ac densos fertur moriturus in hostis.
sentences.l:
As of the city captured the fall and torn-up he saw
thresholds of the roofs and the enemy in the midst in the inner rooms,
arms long unaccustomed the old man, to trembling with age
shoulders puts around in vain, and the useless iron
is girt, and into dense enemies is borne, about to die.
sentences.i: When he saw the fall of the captured city, the doorways of his house torn open and the enemy standing in the heart of his halls, the old man, long unused to arms, buckled them in vain on shoulders that shook with age, strapped on a useless sword, and went, a dying man, into the thick of the foe.
sentences.n: One long sentence. 'uti' is the old form of 'ut', 'when'; its verb is 'vidit', with three objects: 'casum', 'limina convolsa' (the participle 'convolsa' is Greenough's spelling of 'convulsa', 'torn up') and 'hostem'. 'medium in penetralibus hostem' is 'the enemy in the middle, in the inner rooms'. The main verbs are 'circumdat', 'cingitur' and 'fertur'. 'trementibus aevo' goes with 'umeris', 'shoulders trembling with age' (ablative of cause). 'cingitur' is passive in form but middle in sense, 'girds on', with accusative object 'ferrum' (iron, that is, a sword). 'moriturus' is a future participle, 'about to die'. 'densos hostis' is the accusative plural in -is.

sentences.t:
Aedibus in mediis nudoque sub aetheris axe
ingens ara fuit iuxtaque veterrima laurus,
incumbens arae atque umbra complexa Penatis.
sentences.l:
In the middle of the house and under the bare axis of the sky
a huge altar was, and next to it a very ancient laurel,
leaning over the altar and with shade embracing the Penates.
sentences.i: In the midst of the palace, beneath the open vault of heaven, stood a great altar, and beside it a laurel of great age, leaning over the altar and wrapping the household gods in its shade.
sentences.n: A courtyard open to the sky. 'Aedibus in mediis' puts the preposition between adjective and noun. 'nudo… aetheris axe' is 'under the bare pole (vault) of the heavens'; 'aetheris' is a Greek genitive. 'veterrima' is a superlative, 'very old'. 'incumbens' and 'complexa' agree with 'laurus'; 'complexa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'complector', present in sense. 'Penatis' is the accusative plural in -is, the household gods, whose images are mentioned at 517.

sentences.t:
Hic Hecuba et natae nequiquam altaria circum,
praecipites atra ceu tempestate columbae,
condensae et divom amplexae simulacra sedebant.
sentences.l:
Here Hecuba and her daughters in vain the altars around,
headlong in black as if by storm doves,
packed together and the gods' embracing images sat.
sentences.i: Here Hecuba and her daughters sat in vain about the altars, like doves driven headlong by a black storm, crowded together, clasping the images of the gods.
sentences.n: 'altaria circum' puts the preposition after its noun (anastrophe). The simile of doves is given in a few words: 'praecipites atra ceu tempestate columbae', 'like doves, headlong in a black storm'; 'ceu' means 'like, as'. 'condensae' is a perfect participle with passive sense, 'packed close'. 'divom' is the old genitive plural in -um/-om (you'll see this constantly). 'amplexae', as before, is the perfect participle of a deponent with present sense.

sentences.t:
Ipsum autem sumptis Priamum iuvenalibus armis
ut vidit, “Quae mens tam dira, miserrime coniunx,
impulit his cingi telis? Aut quo ruis?
sentences.l:
Himself, however, with taken youthful arms Priam
when she saw, “What mind so dire, most wretched husband,
has driven you with these weapons to be girt? Or whither do you rush?”
sentences.i: But when she saw Priam himself in the arms of a young man which he had put on, “What dreadful resolve, my poor husband, has driven you to gird on these weapons? Where are you rushing off to?”
sentences.n: 'sumptis iuvenalibus armis' is an ablative absolute, but loosely: 'Priam with the arms of youth taken up'. The subject of 'vidit' is Hecuba, named at 515. The speech opens inside line 519, and the verb of speaking, 'inquit', is put off to 520. 'mens' is 'mind, resolve, purpose'. 'impulit' takes 'te' to be understood, with the passive infinitive 'cingi' (middle in sense, 'to gird yourself'); 'his telis' is an ablative of means. 'quo ruis' is 'whither do you rush headlong?'. Greenough prints a space before the closing mark (`ruis? ”inquit`), so the ” heads the `t` of the next unit and is carried in this unit's `l` and `i`.

sentences.i: she said; “Not help like this, nor defenders such as these, does the hour demand—no, not if my own Hector were here beside us.
sentences.n: The ” opening this unit's `t` closes Hecuba's first speech; the second begins on the same line. 'eget' takes the ablative ('tali auxilio… defensoribus istis'), 'has need of'. 'tempus' is the crisis of the time. 'non, si… adforet' means 'not even if…': 'adforet' is the form of 'adesset' (imperfect subjunctive, a condition contrary to fact). 'ipse meus Hector' puts the stress on 'my Hector himself'.

sentences.t: Huc tandem concede;
sentences.l: Hither at last withdraw;
sentences.i: Come over here at last;
sentences.n: 'concede' is the imperative of 'concedo', here 'withdraw, come away'. 'huc' is 'to this place', that is, to the altar; 'tandem' marks impatience.

sentences.t:
haec ara tuebitur omnis,
aut moriere simul.
sentences.l:
this altar will protect all,
or you will die together.
sentences.i: this altar will shelter us all, or you will die with us.
sentences.n: 'omnis' is the accusative plural in -is, 'all (of us)'. 'moriere' is the second person singular future of 'morior', with the older ending -ere for -eris (not the -ere for -erunt noted before). 'simul' is 'together', understood 'with us'. Greenough prints a space before the closing mark (`simul. ”Sic`), so the ” heads the `t` of the next unit and is carried in this unit's `l` and `i`: Hecuba's speech ends here.

sentences.t:
”Sic ore effata recepit
ad sese et sacra longaevum in sede locavit.
sentences.l:
Thus with her mouth having spoken she received
to herself, and in the holy seat the aged man placed.
sentences.i: So she spoke, drew him to her, and seated the aged king in that holy place.
sentences.n: The ” opening this unit's `t` closes Hecuba's second speech. 'effata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'effor', 'having spoken' (you'll see this constantly); 'ore' is the ablative of means, 'with her mouth'. 'recepit ad sese' is 'took him to herself' (the object 'eum', Priam, is understood and is picked up by 'longaevum', 'the aged one', at 525). 'sacra sede' is an ablative of place where.

sentences.t:
Ecce autem elapsus Pyrrhi de caede Polites,
unus natorum Priami, per tela, per hostis
porticibus longis fugit, et vacua atria lustrat
saucius:
sentences.l:
Behold, however, escaped from Pyrrhus' slaughter Polites,
one of the sons of Priam, through weapons, through enemies
by long colonnades flees, and the empty halls scans
wounded:
sentences.i: But see—Polites, one of Priam's sons, has slipped away from Pyrrhus' butchery, and through spears and through enemies, along the long colonnades, he flees, and wounded he crosses the empty halls:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ecce autem' introduces a new turn of the story. 'elapsus' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'elabor', 'having slipped away'. 'natorum' is the old contracted genitive plural. 'hostis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is. 'porticibus longis' is a poetic ablative of the way along which, without a preposition. 'lustrat' means 'traverses, surveys'. 'saucius' is the nominative, 'wounded', and the colon leads to the pursuit.

sentences.t:
illum ardens infesto volnere Pyrrhus
insequitur, iam iamque manu tenet et premit hasta.
sentences.l:
him blazing with hostile wound Pyrrhus
pursues, now and now with his hand he holds and presses with spear.
sentences.i: Pyrrhus, aflame, follows hard on him with a threatening thrust, and every moment has him in his grip and presses him with the spear.
sentences.n: 'illum' is the object of 'insequitur', placed first. 'ardens' is a present participle, 'blazing' with rage. 'infesto volnere' is an ablative of means, 'with a hostile wound', that is, ready to strike (Greenough's spelling 'volnere'; the Latin Library 'vulnere'). 'iam iamque' means 'at any moment now'; 'tenet' and 'premit' are presents, 'has hold of… presses'. 'manu' is 'in his hand'; 'hasta' an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Ut tandem ante oculos evasit et ora parentum,
concidit, ac multo vitam cum sanguine fudit.
sentences.l:
When at last before the eyes and faces of his parents he came out,
he collapsed, and much life with blood poured out.
sentences.i: When at last he reached the sight and faces of his parents, he fell, and poured out his life in a flood of blood.
sentences.n: 'ut' with the perfect indicative 'evasit' means 'when'. 'ante oculos et ora' is 'before the eyes and faces'. 'concidit' is the perfect of 'concido', 'fell down', and 'fudit' the perfect of 'fundo', 'poured out'. 'vitam cum sanguine' puts life and blood side by side; 'multo' goes with 'sanguine'.

sentences.t:
Hic Priamus, quamquam in media iam morte tenetur,
non tamen abstinuit, nec voci iraeque pepercit:
sentences.l:
Here Priam, although in the middle now of death he is held,
not however held back, nor for voice and anger spared:
sentences.i: At this Priam, though he was already held in the very midst of death, did not hold back, nor spare his voice or his anger:
sentences.n: 'quamquam' takes the indicative, 'tenetur'. 'in media morte' is 'in the middle of death'. 'abstinuit' is used without an object, 'held back'. 'voci iraeque' are datives with 'pepercit', a verb of sparing, which takes the dative. The colon introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
“At tibi pro scelere, exclamat, pro talibus ausis,
di, si qua est caelo pietas, quae talia curet,
persolvant grates dignas et praemia reddant
debita, qui nati coram me cernere letum
fecisti et patrios foedasti funere voltus.
sentences.l:
“But to you for the crime, he cries out, for such daring deeds,
gods, if any in heaven is duty, which such things may care for,
may repay thanks worthy and rewards render
due, who of the son in front of me to see the death
you made and the fathers defiled with death countenance.
sentences.i: “For this wickedness, for such daring, may the gods—if there is any justice in heaven that cares about such things—pay you in full the thanks you have earned, and give you the rewards that are your due, you who made me look upon my own son's death, and soiled a father's face with a corpse.
sentences.n: The speech opens at 535, with the verb of speaking ('exclamat') inside it. 'At' introduces an imprecation, a curse. The wish is expressed by the present subjunctive 'persolvant… reddant', with 'di' (= 'dii') as subject and 'tibi' as dative. 'si qua est caelo pietas' is 'if there is any pietas in heaven', where 'pietas' is the gods' sense of duty and justice. 'quae talia curet' is a relative clause with the subjunctive, 'such as to care for such things'. 'grates dignas' and 'praemia debita' are bitterly ironical: what he deserves is punishment. 'qui… fecisti' is 'you who made'; 'fecisti' takes the infinitive 'cernere' with 'me' ('coram me', 'before my eyes'). 'funere' is an ablative of means, the 'death' (here the corpse). 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library 'vultus').

sentences.t:
At non ille, satum quo te mentiris, Achilles
talis in hoste fuit Priamo;
sentences.l:
But not that one, born of whom you falsely claim yourself, Achilles,
such toward an enemy was Priam;
sentences.i: But that Achilles, whose son you falsely say you are, was not such to Priam, his foe;
sentences.n: 'satum quo' is 'sprung from whom', the participle 'satum' (from 'sero') agreeing with 'te'. 'te mentiris' means 'you falsely claim yourself (to be)'; 'mentior' is a deponent verb. 'talis in hoste… Priamo' is 'such toward Priam as a foe'; 'in' with the ablative means 'in the case of'. Priam refers to Achilles' conduct in the last book of the Iliad.

sentences.t:
sed iura fidemque
supplicis erubuit, corpusque exsangue sepulchro
reddidit Hectoreum, meque in mea regna remisit.”
sentences.l:
but the rights and the faith
of a suppliant he blushed at, and the body bloodless to the tomb
restored, Hector's, and me into my kingdom sent back.”
sentences.i: but he honoured the rights and trust due a suppliant, gave Hector's bloodless body back for burial, and sent me home to my own kingdom.”
sentences.n: 'erubuit' takes the accusative, 'blushed before, respected'. 'iura fidemque supplicis' are 'the rights and the good faith of a suppliant'. 'sepulchro' is a dative of purpose or direction, 'for the tomb' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library 'sepulcro'). 'Hectoreum' is the adjective 'of Hector'. The speech closes with the mark Greenough prints after the full stop. The Homeric model is Iliad 24, where Priam begs Achilles for Hector's body.

sentences.t:
Sic fatus senior, telumque imbelle sine ictu
coniecit, rauco quod protinus aere repulsum
e summo clipei nequiquam umbone pependit.
sentences.l:
Thus having spoken the old man, and a weapon unwarlike without a blow
hurled, which at once by hoarse bronze repelled
from the top of the shield in vain by the boss hung.
sentences.i: So the old man spoke, and hurled a spear that had no war in it and no force behind the blow; the hoarse bronze turned it at once, and it hung, to no purpose, from the upper boss of the shield.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sic fatus' is the perfect participle of a deponent, 'having thus spoken'. 'imbelle' is 'unwarlike', and 'sine ictu' 'without a stroke' (the throw had no strength). 'quod' is a plain relative, 'which'. 'rauco aere' is an ablative of cause, 'by the hoarse bronze' (the sound of the shield). 'e summo… umbone' is 'from the top of the boss', and 'clipei' depends on 'umbone'. 'pependit' is the perfect of 'pendeo', 'hang', not of 'pendo'. Greenough prints 'e' where the Latin Library has 'et'; 'et' would add a word but not change the sense.

sentences.t:
Cui Pyrrhus: “Referes ergo haec et nuntius ibis
Pelidae genitori;
sentences.l:
To him Pyrrhus: “You will report therefore these things and a messenger you will go
to Peleus' son, my father;
sentences.i: To him Pyrrhus: “Then you shall report this, and go as my messenger to the son of Peleus, my father;
sentences.n: 'Cui' is a connecting relative, 'to whom (Pyrrhus said)', with the verb of speaking understood (you'll see this constantly). 'Referes' and 'ibis' are futures used as commands. 'nuntius' is predicative, 'as a messenger'. 'Pelidae' is a Greek dative, 'to the son of Peleus', that is, Achilles, in apposition to 'genitori'. Priam is told to go as a messenger to the underworld.

sentences.t:
illi mea tristia facta
degeneremque Neoptolemum narrare memento.
sentences.l:
to him my grim deeds
and degenerate Neoptolemus to tell remember.
sentences.i: remember to tell him of my grim deeds, and of Neoptolemus, his degenerate son.
sentences.n: 'memento' is the future imperative of 'memini', 'remember', here with the infinitive 'narrare'. 'illi' is a dative with 'narrare'. 'degeneremque Neoptolemum' answers Priam's taunt at 540–541: if the son is unworthy, let Achilles be told so. 'tristia facta' are 'grim deeds'.

sentences.t: Nunc morere.
sentences.l: Now die.
sentences.i: Now die.
sentences.n: 'morere' is the singular imperative of the deponent 'morior'. After a speech with long clauses the command is two words.

sentences.t:
”Hoc dicens altaria ad ipsa trementem
traxit et in multo lapsantem sanguine nati,
implicuitque comam laeva, dextraque coruscum
extulit, ac lateri capulo tenus abdidit ensem.
sentences.l:
”This saying, to the altars themselves, trembling,
he dragged, and slipping in much blood of his son,
and wound his hair in his left, and with right the gleaming
raised, and to the side up to the hilt buried the sword.
sentences.i: With these words he dragged him, shaking, to the very altar, slipping in the pools of his son's blood, twisted his left hand in the old man's hair, raised the flashing sword in his right, and buried it in his side up to the hilt.
sentences.n: Greenough prints a space before the closing mark (`morere. ”Hoc`), so the ” closing Pyrrhus' speech heads this unit's `t`. 'Hoc dicens' is 'saying this'. 'trementem' and 'lapsantem' agree with Priam, who is the unstated object of 'traxit'. 'in multo sanguine nati' is 'in the much blood of his son'. 'laeva' is an ablative, 'with his left (hand)', and 'dextra' likewise. 'coruscum' and 'ensem' frame the clause (hyperbaton): 'the flashing… sword'. 'capulo tenus' is 'as far as the hilt': 'tenus' comes after its ablative. 'lateri' is a dative of the place into which.

sentences.t: Haec finis Priami fatorum;
sentences.l: This the end of Priam's fates;
sentences.i: Such was the closing of Priam's destiny;
sentences.n: The first half of a famous passage. 'Haec finis Priami fatorum' has no verb, 'est' being understood. 'finis' can be masculine or feminine; here it agrees with 'haec'. 'fatorum' is a genitive plural, 'of the fates'.

sentences.t:
hic exitus illum
sorte tulit, Troiam incensam et prolapsa videntem
Pergama, tot quondam populis terrisque superbum
regnatorem Asiae.
sentences.l:
this exit him
by lot carried off, Troy burned and fallen seeing
Pergamum, over so many once peoples and lands proud
ruler of Asia.
sentences.i: this was the end that his lot brought him to, who had seen Troy set on fire and Pergamum sink, once proud ruler of Asia over so many peoples and lands.
sentences.n: 'hic exitus illum sorte tulit' is 'this end carried him off by lot', and 'sorte' is an ablative of means. 'videntem' is a present participle agreeing with 'illum', with the objects 'Troiam incensam' and 'Pergama prolapsa'. 'Pergama' is the neuter plural, the citadel. 'tot… populis terrisque' is an ablative with 'superbum', 'proud in the possession of'. 'regnatorem' is in apposition with 'illum'.

sentences.t:
Iacet ingens litore truncus,
avolsumque umeris caput, et sine nomine corpus.
sentences.l:
Lies huge on the shore a trunk,
and torn from the shoulders a head, and without a name a body.
sentences.i: On the beach lies a great trunk, a head wrenched from the shoulders, a body with no name.
sentences.n: 'Iacet' begins the sentence; 'truncus' is its subject, with 'caput' and 'corpus' joined by 'et' and understood 'iacent'. 'litore' is an ablative of place where without a preposition. 'avolsum' is Greenough's spelling of 'avulsum', 'torn away'. 'sine nomine' ('without a name') means that the body cannot be recognised, or that the king is now nobody.

sentences.t: At me tum primum saevus circumstetit horror.
sentences.l: But me then first a savage shuddering stood around.
sentences.i: Then, for the first time, a savage horror closed in around me.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. Aeneas turns from the story of Priam to his own state. 'circumstetit' is a compound verb which takes an accusative object, 'me'. 'tum primum' is 'then for the first time', not having been frightened until this sight of a king's death. 'saevus horror' is a 'fierce shuddering'.

sentences.t: Obstipui;
sentences.l: I was stunned;
sentences.i: I stood dumb;
sentences.n: 'Obstipui' is the perfect of 'obstipesco' (or 'obstupesco'), 'I was struck dumb'. One word forms the whole sentence.

sentences.i: the image of my dear father rose before me, as I saw the king, of his own years, breathing out his life from a cruel wound;
sentences.n: 'subiit' is the perfect of 'subeo', 'came up (into the mind)'; it is repeated at the beginning of the next clause (anaphora). 'ut… vidi' is 'when I saw', 'ut' with the perfect indicative. 'aequaevum' means 'of the same age' as Anchises. 'exhalantem' is a present participle agreeing with 'regem', 'breathing out'. 'volnere' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnere', an ablative of means or source.

sentences.t:
subiit deserta Creüsa,
et direpta domus, et parvi casus Iuli.
sentences.l:
came up abandoned Creusa,
and the plundered house, and of little Iulus the fortune.
sentences.i: there rose to mind Creusa, left alone, my plundered house, and the peril of little Iulus.
sentences.n: 'deserta' is a perfect participle, 'abandoned, left behind'. 'Creüsa' is Aeneas' wife; the diaeresis ('ü') shows that the 'e' and 'u' are sounded apart in three syllables. 'direpta' is 'plundered'. 'casus' is 'fortune, hazard', here the danger Iulus is in. 'parvi Iuli' is the genitive of Iulus (also called Ascanius). The three sentences are built the same way: the three objects of tender concern.

sentences.t: Respicio, et quae sit me circum copia lustro.
sentences.l: I look back, and what there is around me of force I survey.
sentences.i: I look back and survey what force stands about me.
sentences.n: 'Respicio' is a present, 'I look back'. 'quae sit… copia' is an indirect question, 'what force there is', with 'sit' subjunctive; 'copia' here means 'band, number of men'. 'me circum' puts the preposition after its pronoun.

sentences.t:
Deseruere omnes defessi, et corpora saltu
ad terram misere aut ignibus aegra dedere.
sentences.l:
Deserted all, exhausted, and bodies by a leap
to the ground they sent, or to the fires, sick, gave.
sentences.i: All had left me, worn out; some had flung their bodies from the roof to the ground, others had given up their weary frames to the flames.
sentences.n: 'Deseruere', 'misere' and 'dedere' are perfects in -ere for -erunt (you'll see this constantly). 'omnes' is the nominative plural, 'all'. 'defessi' is 'worn out'. 'saltu' is an ablative of means, 'by a leap'. 'aegra' agrees with 'corpora', 'worn, spent'. 'ignibus dedere' means 'gave up to the flames'.

sentences.t:
[Iamque adeo super unus eram, cum limina Vestae]
[servantem et tacitam secreta in sede latentem]
[Tyndarida aspicio: dant clara incendia lucem]
[erranti passimque oculos per cuncta ferenti.]
sentences.l:
[And now indeed over alone I was, when the threshold of Vesta]
[guarding and silent in a secret seat lurking]
[the Tyndarid I behold: give bright fires light]
[to me wandering and everywhere eyes through all things carrying.]
sentences.i: [And now I was the only one left, when I saw the daughter of Tyndareus, keeping watch at Vesta's threshold, silent, hidden in a secluded place; the bright fires gave light to me as I wandered and turned my eyes everywhere.]
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the start of the bracketed stretch: Greenough brackets 2.567–588 as spurious (line 588 falls in the next part), and every line here is printed inside [ ], which the `t` keeps. The lines are missing from the best manuscripts, and the ancient commentator Servius says Varius and Tucca removed them; they are given here as Greenough prints them. 'super… eram' is 'supereram', 'I was left over' (tmesis, a word cut in two). 'adeo' is an intensifier, 'by this time'. 'Vestae limina servantem' is 'guarding the threshold of Vesta's shrine'. 'Tyndarida' is a Greek accusative, 'daughter of Tyndareus', Helen. 'clara' agrees with 'incendia', 'bright fires' (the Latin Library 'claram' would agree with 'lucem', 'a bright light'; either way the fires are bright). 'erranti' and 'ferenti' are present participles in the dative, agreeing with the 'mihi' understood, 'to me as I wandered… carrying my eyes'. 'oculos ferre' is 'to turn the eyes'.

sentences.t:
[Illa sibi infestos eversa ob Pergama Teucros]
[et poenas Danaum et deserti coniugis iras]
[praemetuens, Troiae et patriae communis Erinys,]
[abdiderat sese atque aris invisa sedebat.]
sentences.l:
[She, to herself hostile, because of overthrown Pergamum, the Teucrians]
[and the penalties of the Danaans and of her abandoned husband the angers]
[fearing in advance, of Troy and of her country common Fury,]
[had hidden herself and at the altars hated sat.]
sentences.i: [Fearing in advance the Trojans, bitter against her for the overthrow of Pergamum, the Greeks' vengeance, and the anger of the husband she had deserted—the common Fury of Troy and of her own country—she had hidden herself, and sat hated at the altars.]
sentences.n: 'Illa' is the subject of both 'abdiderat' and 'sedebat'. 'praemetuens' takes three objects: 'Teucros', 'poenas', 'iras'. 'sibi infestos' means 'hostile to her' (dative of reference). 'eversa ob Pergama' is 'because of Pergamum overthrown'. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural. The Latin Library has 'poenam' (singular) for Greenough's 'poenas'; the sense is the same, 'the penalty of the Greeks'. 'deserti coniugis' is Menelaus, whom she left for Paris. 'Erinys' is a Greek word, 'a Fury'; Helen is called one because she has brought ruin to both Troy and Greece. 'aris invisa' is 'hated at the altars'.

sentences.t:
[Exarsere ignes animo; subit ira cadentem]
[ulcisci patriam et sceleratas sumere poenas.]
sentences.l:
[Blazed up fires in my mind; comes anger the falling]
[to avenge fatherland and criminal to take penalties.]
sentences.i: [Fires flared up in my mind; anger rose in me to avenge my falling country and exact the penalty due a criminal.]
sentences.n: 'Exarsere' is the perfect 'exarserunt' (-ere = -erunt). 'animo' is an ablative of place, 'in my mind'. 'subit ira' takes the infinitives 'ulcisci' and 'sumere', 'anger comes (to me) to avenge… and to take'; 'ulcisci' is a deponent infinitive. 'cadentem' agrees with 'patriam', 'falling'. 'sceleratas poenas' are the penalties exacted for a crime, 'sumere poenas' being the idiom 'to exact penalty'.

sentences.t:
[“Scilicet haec Spartam incolumis patriasque Mycenas]
[aspiciet, partoque ibit regina triumpho,]
[coniugiumque, domumque, patres, natosque videbit,]
[Iliadum turba et Phrygiis comitata ministris?]
sentences.l:
[“Of course she Sparta safe and Mycenae of her fathers]
[will behold, and with a triumph won will go as queen,]
[and husband, and house, fathers, and sons will see,]
[of Trojan women with a crowd and by Phrygian attendants accompanied?]
sentences.i: [“Is she, then, to see Sparta and her ancestral Mycenae unharmed, go off as a queen in a triumph she has won, and see husband and house, parents and children, with a crowd of Trojan women and Phrygian servants in attendance?]
sentences.n: The speech is Aeneas' own, spoken to himself, and opens inside the bracket with “ at 577. 'Scilicet' here is ironical, 'of course'. 'haec' is 'this woman', Helen. 'incolumis' is a nominative, 'safe, unharmed'. 'patrias' is loosely used for the 'ancestral' cities: Sparta (Menelaus') and Mycenae (Agamemnon's). 'partoque triumpho' is an ablative absolute, 'a triumph having been won'. Greenough prints 'patres', 'parents' (the Latin Library 'patris' would give 'her father's' and so bring in Tyndareus alone). 'Iliadum' is a Greek genitive plural, 'of the women of Ilium'. 'comitata' is a deponent participle used passively, 'accompanied'. The question has no particle, 'aspiciet… ibit… videbit' being the future with the force of an indignant 'Is she to…?'.

sentences.t: [Occiderit ferro Priamus, Troia arserit igni?]
sentences.l: [Will have fallen by the sword Priam, Troy burned with fire?]
sentences.i: [And all the while Priam is to have died by the sword, Troy to have burned in fire?]
sentences.n: 'Occiderit… arserit' are perfect subjunctives in an indignant question ('Is it to be that…?'), with no introductory word; the clauses are linked without 'et' (asyndeton). 'ferro' and 'igni' are ablatives of means.

sentences.t: [Dardanium totiens sudarit sanguine litus?]
sentences.l: [Dardanian so often shall have sweated with blood the shore?]
sentences.i: [And the Dardan shore to have run so often with blood?]
sentences.n: 'sudarit' is the syncopated form of 'sudaverit', a perfect subjunctive in the same indignant question. 'Dardanium litus' is the 'Dardan (Trojan) shore'. 'sudo' means 'sweat', so the shore itself 'sweats' blood. 'totiens' is 'so often'.

sentences.t:
[Non ita: namque etsi nullum memorabile nomen]
[feminea in poena est, nec habet victoria laudem,]
[extinxisse nefas tamen et sumpsisse merentis]
[laudabor poenas, animumque explesse iuvabit]
[ultricis flammae, et cineres satiasse meorum.”]
sentences.l:
[Not so: for although no memorable name]
[in a woman's punishment is, nor does victory have praise,]
[to have extinguished a crime, yet, and to have exacted of the deserving]
[I shall be praised penalties, and to have filled my spirit it will please]
[of avenging flame, and the ashes of my own to have sated.”]
sentences.i: [No, it shall not be so. For though there is no famous name in punishing a woman, and no praise in such a victory, I shall be praised all the same for having wiped out a crime and exacted the penalty from one who deserves it; and it will be a joy to have filled my spirit with avenging flame and satisfied the ashes of my own.”]
sentences.n: The speech ends with ” at 587, inside the bracket. 'Non ita' is 'not so', answering the questions above. 'etsi' is concessive, with the indicative 'est' and 'habet'. 'nullum memorabile nomen' is the subject of 'est', 'there is no memorable name in (the punishing of) a woman'. The Latin Library has 'haec' for Greenough's 'nec', which would reverse the sense ('and this victory has praise'); the sense of 'nec' is clear from the 'etsi'. 'laudabor' is followed by the perfect infinitives 'extinxisse' and 'sumpsisse', 'I shall be praised (for) having…'; 'merentis' is the participle of 'mereo' used as a noun, 'those who deserve it'. 'iuvabit' is impersonal, with the infinitives 'explesse' (= 'explevisse') and 'satiasse' (= 'satiavisse') as subjects. 'ultricis flammae' is a genitive with 'explesse' (verbs of filling take the genitive). The Latin Library has 'famam' (fame) for Greenough's 'flammae' (the fire of vengeance); we keep 'flammae'. 'cineres meorum' are the ashes (the shades) of his own people, satisfied by vengeance.
